doc.title: Frank Wess interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

title: Riff style and music being played before it is written
summary: Wess says bands start with head arrangements, as with Eckstine's band and Joe Williams's 'Every Day', since music is played before written.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Can you tell us anything about or contrast for us, what they call the riff style, that they played in the bands in the southwest, as compared to the big bands on the east coast.
I don’t know what that is. I don’t know. I don’t know, people name things, I don’t know what it is.
I guess they call it the Kansas City style of creating riffs and so forth.

Well that’s, bands, they’ve done that. All bands, most bands when they first start out, you know they start out like that because they don’t have any music, so you’ve got to start like that, you know. When I was with Billy Eckstine’s band, it started out the same way, you know. You start out, you’ve got two or three arrangements and you’ve got to do a job four or five hours, and you’ve got to have a book so you make up music as you go. That arrangement on “Every Day” that Joe Williams did, the band was playing it a head. When Joe Williams came in the band, he didn’t have no music. Basie played the introduction and we started playing the music. And Ernie Wilkins just put an introduction on it, and copied just what we played, he wrote just what we played.
That’s great. That’s like arranging in reverse almost.

Well that’s the way it is always. Music is always played before it’s written. So it’s usually that’s the reason when you see something written a certain way, whoever wrote it meant for it to sound the way he heard it. See because it comes from the playing, not the writing to the playing, from the playing to the writing. That’s the way it usually goes. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
You know they also say that is true with the arrangers. The arrangers basically they say listen to the soloist.
That’s what I mean. Yeah. That’s what I mean. Yeah. They hear it, and then they write it.
